item.title: Week 8: Stuck at Every Step
item.description:
Oil and water don’t mix. Neither do combinatorics and me — yet.

What I did

  • Stat 110:
    • lecture 2 on story proofs and the axioms of probability
    • Strategic Practice 1 — counting with dice, palindromes, and poker hands (flush, two pair), lattice paths, the probability that a random word with no repeated letters uses the whole alphabet (it’s very close to 1/e), and story proofs
  • Probability by hand: 1 of 3 sessions
  • OpenStax Biology 2e: chapter 4 on cell structure — studying cells with microscopes, prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells, the endomembrane system, the cytoskeleton, and connections between cells
  • MIT 7.01SC Fundamentals of Biology: the first 4 lessons of unit 1, Biochemistry — types of organisms and what cells are made of, covalent and hydrogen bonds, macromolecules (lipids, carbohydrates, nucleic acids), and proteins with their levels of structure and the non-covalent forces that hold them together
  • Field reading: following researchers and journals on Bluesky, Google Scholar alerts for my keywords
  • Khan Academy, High School Biology: 2 hours and 30 minutes, going through unit 5 on gene expression and regulation
  • English Pronunciation in Use: units 1–2
  • Academic Vocabulary in Use: units 7–11 on
    • key quantifying expressions
    • words with several meanings
    • metaphors and idioms
    • nouns and the words they combine with
    • adjective and noun combinations
  • English Grammar in Use Intermediate: units 12–14 on present perfect and past simple
  • Shadowing: six 15-minute sessions
  • IELTS practice tests: Reading 32/40 (band 7.0), Listening 35/40 (band 8.0)

What clicked

Fat isn’t hydrophobic — water is fat-phobic. Water molecules can’t form hydrogen bonds with nonpolar tails, so around each tail they have to arrange themselves into an ordered “cage” and lose their freedom of movement (entropy). It’s more favorable for water to push all the nonpolar molecules into one cluster, which shrinks the surface it has to organize around. The oil doesn’t avoid water; water squeezes the oil out. Fat-shaming at the molecular level.

Where I got stuck

Stat 110, Strategic Practice 1 — pretty much everywhere. Dice, palindromes, poker hands, lattice paths, words without repeated letters, story proofs: I got stuck at almost every step of every problem and couldn’t have solved any of them without hints. Counting turned out to be a completely different way of thinking from anything I’d done before. Each problem needs its own way of looking at it, and I don’t have a toolbox for that yet.

What worked was taking one hint at a time and then trying the next step myself. It was slow, but by the end, I could at least see which questions to ask: does order matter, am I counting something twice, can I count the complement instead?

What I’m changing

  • Stat 110 problems in shorter, more frequent sessions. Long sessions on counting problems left me stuck and frustrated. Starting next week, I’m switching from three 40-minute sessions to six 20-minute ones: less time to spiral on a single step, more chances to come back with fresh eyes.
  • Back to basic chemistry. Biochemistry kept assuming things I didn’t remember from school: electronegativity, ionic and covalent bonds, polarity, hydrogen bonds. Alongside the main courses, I’m spending time on the basics with Crash Course Chemistry and Khan Academy.
  • Calculus starts. The next course on my route is Differential and Integral Calculus, so derivatives and integrals join the weekly plan.

item.title: Week 7: Chickens, Eggs, and Adenine
item.description:
Mendel’s second law says alleles are independent. My understanding of LIA was not.

What I did

  • Python for Data Analysis: chapters 4–6, NumPy arrays and vectorized computation, getting started with pandas (Series and DataFrame), and loading and saving data in different file formats.
  • Rosalind: problems 11–15, mortal rabbits (FIBD), overlap graphs for DNA sequences (GRPH), expected offspring (IEV), the longest common substring of several sequences (LCSM), and Mendel’s second law with the binomial distribution (LIA).
  • Stat 110: lecture 1 and chapter 1, probability and counting — the naive definition of probability, multiplication rule, binomial coefficients, and story proofs.
  • The Linux Command Line: chapter 18, archiving and backup — compressing files with gzip and bzip2, packing them with tar and zip, and syncing directories with rsync.
  • Linear algebra by hand: 3 of 3 sessions, solving systems of linear equations with Gaussian elimination, including systems with parameters.
  • Khan Academy, High School Biology: 5 hours and 40 minutes, completed unit 4
  • Academic Vocabulary in Use: unit 6 on phrasal verbs
  • English Grammar in Use Intermediate: unit 11 on present perfect
  • IELTS practice tests: Listening 36/40 (band 8.0), Reading 33/40 (band 7.5)

What clicked

Common doesn’t mean original. I assumed the most common version of a trait must be the ancestral one: brown eyes, for example. It turns out frequency proves nothing, because selection, founder effects, and drift can all make a derived trait common. The ancestral state is found by comparing with an outgroup and reconstructing states along the tree. One part of my intuition survived: breaking is easier than building, so “no pigment” is usually the derived state (blue eyes, white eggs in some chicken breeds).

So which egg came first? The earliest dinosaur eggs were soft and unpigmented. Egg color evolved once, in eumaniraptoran dinosaurs (biliverdin for blue-green, protoporphyrin IX for red-brown), and birds inherited it. The first chicken egg was most likely beige, like the eggs of the red junglefowl.

The A in DNA and the A in ATP are almost the same thing. Both are adenine. ATP is adenine + ribose + three phosphates, and the A in RNA is the same molecule with one phosphate left: RNA polymerase builds RNA directly from ATP, GTP, CTP, and UTP, cleaving off two phosphates to power each new bond. The A in DNA has deoxyribose instead and comes from dATP. The same adenosine shows up in NAD⁺, FAD, coenzyme A, and cAMP. One explanation is the RNA world hypothesis: our energy currency and cofactors may be molecular fossils of a time when RNA did everything.

Lactose tolerance is a broken off switch. In most mammals, the lactase gene (LCT) is turned down after weaning, so lactose intolerance in adults is the original state. Tolerance comes from mutations in a regulatory region, located inside the neighboring gene MCM6, that keep the gene switched on. These mutations arose independently several times (in Europe, East Africa, and the Middle East), a textbook case of convergent evolution.

Where I got stuck

Rosalind LIA. At first I didn’t understand what the problem was asking. I mixed up distributions (Bernoulli is one trial, binomial counts successes in n trials, normal is only an approximation for large n), wrote the binomial coefficient as n!/(k!·(n−1)!) instead of n!/(k!·(n−k)!), and confused “exactly k” with “at least k.” What worked: go step by step with my own formula. First compute “exactly k,” then loop i from 0 to k−1 and take 1 − sum. Lesson: solve one case first, then generalize with a loop.

What I’m changing

  • Stat 110: practice separate from reading. Reading the chapter and watching the lecture wasn’t enough to make the ideas stick. Starting next week, I’ll work through every exercise in the textbook in order, in separate sessions that are only for solving problems.
  • Probability by hand. Three short sessions a week of routine problems until they feel automatic, plus one or two from Mosteller’s Fifty Challenging Problems in Probability — the same approach that worked for linear algebra.

item.title: Week 6: Imaginary Numbers, Real Mistakes
item.description:
Don’t repeat yourself — unless it’s the final check.

What I did

  • Linear algebra by hand: caught up on two weeks at once — six sessions on determinants, complex numbers, Cramer’s rule, and some trigonometry along the way.
  • The Linux Command Line: chapters 14–17, which completes the first two parts of the book.
  • Rosalind: CONS, Consensus and Profile — building a profile matrix from several DNA strings and reading the most common letter at each position.
  • Academic Vocabulary in Use: units 2–5, with new words added to my flashcards.

What clicked

  • Complex numbers in determinants. For a matrix with c + di and c − di in the corners, the product of these two numbers turned out to be just a difference of squares: (c + di)(c − di) = c² − (di)² = c² + d², because i² = −1. A complex number times its conjugate is a plain real number. Once I saw that, determinants with i stopped looking scary.
  • Writing code once and reusing it. For CONS I needed to read FASTA files, so I wrote my own parser and moved it into a separate module. Now every new Rosalind problem starts with one import line instead of copying the same code again.

Where I got stuck

  • Small signs, big errors. I kept writing i² as 1 instead of −1, which flipped the sign of a whole term in the determinant. In the linear systems I solved with Cramer’s rule, the final check didn’t match because of a single sign.
  • Brute-force Python. My CONS solution works, but it’s long and repetitive. I can see that it could be shorter (for example, with zip or lambda), but I’m not at that level of Python yet.
  • FASTA format. One sequence can be split across several lines, and at first it wasn’t obvious how to glue the lines back into a single string.

What I’m changing

  • Always substitute the answer back into the original equations — the check catches exactly the sign mistakes I keep making.
  • Practice Python idioms (zip, dictionaries, lambda) on small exercises, so that my Rosalind solutions become shorter over time.
  • Keep a growing module of my own utilities and reuse it.

Next week

  • Khan Academy, High School Biology: unit 4
  • Readings on the mitochondrial genetic code
  • Python for Data Analysis: chapters 4–6
  • Rosalind: 5 problems
  • The Linux Command Line: chapters 18–21
  • Solving linear algebra problems: 1 hour
  • Alberts: chapter 1
  • R for Data Science: first half of “Whole game”
  • Stat 110: lectures 1–2 + Strategic Practice and Homework 1
  • Academic Vocabulary in Use: units 6–28
  • English Pronunciation in Use Intermediate: units 1–4
  • IELTS Listening, Reading, and Writing mock test
  • English Grammar in Use Intermediate: units 11–20

item.title: Week 5: Pause and Resume
item.description:
Checkpoint reached: rest. Next checkpoint: starting again.

This was my most relaxing week so far — a vacation, even though I spent almost every day at home. I needed some time just for myself. I walked a lot, played The Sims 4, and studied only a little. It’s hard to get back on track after a break like this, but I really needed it.

What I did

  • The Linux Command Line: chapters 10–13. Chapter 10 covers processes — how to see what’s running with ps and top, and how to stop or pause programs with kill and job control. Chapter 11 is about the environment: shell variables, PATH, and the startup files that set everything up when a terminal opens. Chapter 12 is a gentle introduction to vi — enough to open a file, edit it, save, and (most importantly) exit. Chapter 13 shows how to customize the prompt, which finally explained what all those strange symbols in PS1 mean.

  • Rosalind: 3 problems.

    • IPRB, Mendel’s First Law — the probability that two random organisms from a population produce offspring with a dominant allele. This one was more about probability than code: I had to list all possible parent pairs and their chances first.
    • PROT, Translating RNA into Protein — reading an mRNA string three letters at a time and turning each codon into an amino acid until it reaches a stop codon.
    • SUBS, Finding a Motif in DNA — finding every position where a short motif appears in a longer DNA string, including overlapping matches.

  • Khan Academy, High School Biology: 4 days, 45–50 minutes each. I finished Unit 3: The cell cycle and differentiation. It turned out to be quite a hard unit for me: there are a lot of subtle details about how cells divide, and my notes came out long and dense.

  • Biology lectures: listened to 3 lectures during my walks — one on the history of how DNA was discovered, and two on biomolecules: proteins and lipids.

  • English Grammar in Use: units 6–10 — past continuous, present perfect, and the difference between present perfect simple and continuous (I’ve read vs I’ve been reading).

  • Profiles: pinned my main repositories on GitHub with short descriptions and joined Biostars, a Q&A forum for bioinformatics.

What clicked

Rest is part of the work, not a break from it. After four intense weeks I was more tired than I realized, and this week showed me how much I needed a pause. I didn’t stop completely, though: I walked 7.5 km almost every day, kept my workouts, and listened to biology lectures on the way. That kept a thread connecting me to my routine.

Where I got stuck

  • Switching back on. Coming back after a break turned out to be harder than taking it.
  • Almost no IELTS practice: Speaking and Anki were skipped all seven days, and Reading, Listening, and Writing never started.
  • Linear algebra by hand: 0 of 3 sessions. Python for Data Analysis chapter 4 and the review of Molecular Biology lecture 2 also slipped.
  • The Linux Command Line stopped at chapter 13 instead of the planned 15.

What I’m changing

I want to plan the return in advance. Before a break ends, I’ll choose one or two small, easy tasks for the first morning, so that getting started doesn’t feel like a big step.

Next week

Back to the full routine, starting with the tasks that slipped this time:

  • Linear algebra by hand
  • The IELTS blocks
  • Python for Data Analysis: chapter 4

item.title: Week 4: outrun by Rabbits
item.description:
Deoxyribose is just ribose minus one oxygen. Me after a 5 km run: same.

What I did

  • Missing Semester: lecture 9 and the Data Wrangling lecture (2020 edition). This course is over, and although I didn’t do all the command-line exercises, I now know where to look if I get stuck.
  • The Linux Command Line: chapters 1–9. It picks up where Missing Semester left off but goes deeper into the different commands and nuances of the command line.
  • 3Blue1Brown, Essence of Linear Algebra: lessons 9–16. Some of them were like emotional rollercoasters because one minute I thought I fully understood the concept, and the next I didn’t get it at all. Interestingly, the easiest lesson for me was about eigenvalues and eigenvectors, even though the lecturer said that we have to understand all the previous topics to conceptualize this one. Maybe I am good at linear algebra after all :)
  • Python for Data Analysis: chapters 1–3. I went through introductory chapters about common libraries and data structures in Python. Ready to dig into the analysis!
  • Khan Academy’s High School Biology every day for 45 minutes. Still on unit 3, about the cell cycle. There are a lot of new terms, some of which sound too similar to me.
  • Alberts, Molecular Biology of the Cell: went through half of chapter 6 (“From DNA to Protein”) in order to write my next article.
  • Rosalind problems: solved all the introductory problems in Python Village and did 6 problems in Bioinformatics Stronghold.
  • English: I started learning vocabulary for Writing Task 1 to describe graphs more easily, and worked through units 1–5 of Grammar in Use Intermediate and unit 1 of Academic Vocabulary in Use. Also I recorded myself speaking for 2 minutes for Speaking Part 2. I don’t think I made huge progress this week, but speaking definitely feels less awkward now.
  • Outside bioengineering: ran a 5K race in 39 minutes — both goals done: no walking and under 40 minutes!

What clicked

  • Last week I started diving deep into molecular biology and how DNA and RNA are structured, using a diagram. And this week in Alberts I read that RNA contains ribose instead of deoxyribose, and that diagram popped into my head — great feeling.
  • I realized how well Rosalind is designed. First, you work on your algorithmic thinking. Second, you get molecular biology knowledge as you go. And finally, since the problems are so specific, you feel like a real scientist rather than someone solving abstract puzzles.

Where I got stuck

The prize for the worst feeling of the week goes to the Rosalind problem Rabbits and Recurrence Relations. It is a basic algorithmic problem where you have to count how many rabbits there will be after N months, and I spent a huge amount of time trying to solve it. The solution was pretty simple, but I should solve this kind of task with pen and paper first.

I also did not complete the English tasks I expected to finish. But in my defense, I did speak English for at least 14 minutes, which still counts.

What I’m changing

Next week I am going to be on vacation, so I expect to study a bit less, try to relax and come back with more energy.

Next week

  • Write an article “From genes to proteins”
  • The Linux Command Line: chapters 10–15
  • Python for Data Analysis: chapter 4
  • 3 Rosalind problems
  • Solve linear algebra problems: 3 times a week for 20 minutes
  • Khan Academy’s High School Biology every day
  • A lot of English

item.title: Week 3: Missing Semester, almost found
item.description:
I estimated Missing Semester the way every developer estimates a task: “it’ll take a couple of days.”

What I did

  • A deep dive into mitochondria for this blog: why they have their own DNA and how a swallowed bacterium became part of every animal cell.
  • Missing Semester: lectures 2–8. Seven lectures in one week, and the course is nearly finished: one lecture and one bonus topic left. To be honest, I only watched the lectures and read the notes, without doing the exercises. I don’t see much point in inventing artificial terminal tasks for myself — I’d rather practice when a real need comes up.
  • 3Blue1Brown, Essence of Linear Algebra: lessons 7–8 — inverse matrices, column space and null space, and non-square matrices as transformations between dimensions.
  • Khan Academy’s High School Biology every day for 40 minutes. I finished the second unit, on organ systems.
  • Mock IELTS, all four parts, to get an honest baseline for my English plan. I’m around 6.0 overall on a mock test; the goal is 7.5 by next September.
  • Outside bioengineering: three runs this week getting ready for my 5K race on October 18, a lecture on Van Gogh, university biology lectures as a soundtrack for my walks, and a day with my partner’s grandmother for her birthday.

What clicked

  • Evolution is not a design. While studying biology, everything looks perfectly tuned: every system connected to every other, almost like magic. Then it hits you — it’s survivorship bias. We only see the organisms whose variations happened to work; the rest simply didn’t make it.
  • Mitochondria happened once. Every organism that has mitochondria — me, a mushroom, an oak tree, an amoeba — descends from one and the same ancestral cell. A blue whale and the yeast in my bread are distant cousins.
  • “Beyond the Code” turned out to be my favorite lecture of Missing Semester. I expected another lecture about tools, and got an honest talk about the soft skills around programming instead. It’s the lecture I’d recommend to every beginner developer — and after eight years in frontend, I’d recommend it to experienced ones too.

Where I got stuck

The mock IELTS confirmed something obvious: when you don’t live in an English-speaking environment, active skills suffer the most. I read and listen to English a lot, so Listening and Reading held up reasonably well. But I rarely have to speak or write it, and it shows: in Speaking I run out of words when I have to talk for two minutes straight, and in Writing my ideas are fine, but the language stays simpler than I’d like.

What I’m changing

Most of the changes this week are about English: that’s where the mock IELTS showed the biggest gap.

  • Speaking every day, even if only for two minutes. I take one IELTS Part 2 card, set a timer, and talk with my phone recording. Once a week I transcribe one recording and go through the mistakes. Two minutes sounds like nothing, but it’s two minutes more than I used to speak English.
  • Writing on a schedule. One IELTS task every two weeks, alternating Task 1 and Task 2, each reviewed for mistakes.
  • Grammar and vocabulary from the ground up. I’m going through Cambridge’s “in Use” series cover to cover, starting with English Grammar in Use and Academic Vocabulary in Use. They are not exciting, but active skills need something to build on.
  • A real teacher from November. Recordings and books are a good start, but nothing replaces a live conversation.

Next week

  • Missing Semester: lecture 9 and the Data Wrangling lecture from 2020 — finishing the course
  • The Linux Command Line: chapters 1–10
  • Python for Data Analysis: chapters 1–3
  • A few Rosalind problems
  • Khan Academy’s High School Biology every day
  • 3Blue1Brown: lessons 9–16 — finishing the series
  • A lot of English

item.title: The tenants inside every cell
item.description:
Two billion years later, the tenants are still paying rent in ATP.

“The mitochondria is the powerhouse of the cell” is pretty much all I remembered from school biology. Then I started learning it properly and found out that this little organelle has its own DNA, a two-billion-year-old backstory, and a very particular way of being passed down in families. Here’s what surprised me most.

More than a powerhouse

Our cells contain different parts, and each of them has its own job. These parts are called organelles. One of them, the mitochondrion, works as the “powerhouse of the cell”: it breaks down sugars, fats, and sometimes even proteins, and turns them into energy that the cell stores in molecules of adenosine triphosphate, or ATP for short.

Mitochondria are often pictured as beans floating in the fluid inside the cell, the cytosol. But in fact, they are constantly on the move: special motor proteins pull them along the cell’s “skeleton”, called the cytoskeleton. Thanks to this, mitochondria can end up exactly where energy is needed most.

I used to think there was only one mitochondrion in a cell, because that is how cells are usually drawn in diagrams. It turns out that is not true: a cell can contain many mitochondria, and where a lot of energy is needed, there can be several thousand of them in a single cell — for example, in neurons and heart muscle cells. What’s more, mitochondria can divide and fuse with each other, adjusting their number to the cell’s needs.

Swallowed but not broken

Here is one of the most surprising facts: mitochondria have their own DNA! And it is not like the DNA stored in the nucleus. Nuclear DNA is organized into long chromosomes and tucked away behind the nuclear envelope, while mitochondrial DNA is a small ring that lies right inside the organelle. Bacteria have similar circular DNA — and that is no coincidence.

This is explained by the endosymbiotic theory (Roger et al. 2017). About two billion years ago, the ancestors of mitochondria were independent bacteria. At some point a larger cell engulfed one of these bacteria, but did not digest it, and the bacterium stayed alive inside. The result was a mutually beneficial partnership: the larger cell supplied the bacterium with nutrients, and the bacterium turned them into energy. Hence the name: “endo” means inside, and “symbiosis” means living together to the benefit of both.

By the way, the same thing happened to chloroplasts, the organelles that make plants green. They were once bacteria too, just a different kind: cyanobacteria that could photosynthesize.

It would be logical to assume that the other organelles were once bacteria too, swallowed by big Pac-Men. But that is not the case. According to the leading hypothesis, the endoplasmic reticulum, lysosomes and the Golgi apparatus were “molded” out of the cell’s own membrane. Imagine pressing your finger into a balloon: a pocket forms on the surface. If the edges of the pocket closed and it pinched off, you would get a separate bubble wrapped in its own film. That is how, fold by fold, the cell acquired its internal compartments. And that is why these organelles have no DNA of their own, unlike mitochondria, which arrived from outside with theirs.

Moving out of a dangerous neighborhood

But why did almost all the genes move to the nucleus instead of staying inside the mitochondria? The thing is, it is dangerous in there. When mitochondria produce energy, electrons are passed along their inner membrane, like on a conveyor belt. Sometimes an electron jumps off the belt too early and collides with oxygen. This produces unstable, aggressive molecules, such as superoxide or hydrogen peroxide. You can think of them as sparks from a stove that burn through everything nearby.

Inside the nucleus, DNA is safe: it is separated from the rest of the cell by the nuclear envelope, which has two membranes, and it is tightly packed and wound around protective proteins. Mitochondrial DNA, on the other hand, lies right next to the “stove” and is almost “naked”. Moreover, DNA repair systems are weaker in mitochondria than in the nucleus, so some of the damage stays unrepaired.

As a result, only 37 genes remain in human mitochondrial DNA (Anderson et al. 1981). It is more beneficial to keep them inside, so that each organelle can adjust its energy production to its own needs without waiting for a command from the nucleus (Allen 2015).

These 37 genes are where my December project begins. I am going to take the mitochondrial genomes of humans, mice, fish, flies and yeast and analyze them: why the yeast genome is several times longer than ours even though it has almost the same number of genes, what order the genes are in around the ring, and how mitochondria read the genetic code in their own way, slightly differently from the rest of the cell.

Hand-me-downs from Mom

And here is a fact that surprised me even more: we inherit almost all of our mitochondria from our moms! A child gets half of its nuclear DNA from its dad, but everything else in the cell, including the mitochondria, comes from the egg. In fact, the egg holds the record for mitochondria: a single egg contains about a hundred thousand of them (Babayev and Seli 2015)!

A sperm cell has mitochondria too — they sit at the base of its tail, where they power its swim to the finish line. But after fertilization, the mother’s egg marks the father’s mitochondria as unnecessary, and they are soon destroyed (Sutovsky et al. 1999). Meanwhile, the egg’s own mitochondria remain and supply the embryo’s first cells with energy while they are still in fieri. So that is yet another reason to thank your mom!

Summing up

Put it all together, and it sounds almost like science fiction: every one of our cells is home to the descendants of bacteria that were once swallowed but never digested. They still keep their own DNA, work for us, and are passed down only from our mothers. In school, the mitochondrion was just a line for me: “the powerhouse of the cell”. It turned out to be a two-billion-year-long story.

I wonder what else in the cell will turn out to be different from how it’s drawn in diagrams.

References

Allen, John F. 2015. “Why Chloroplasts and Mitochondria Retain Their Own Genomes and Genetic Systems: Colocation for Redox Regulation of Gene Expression.” Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America 112 (33): 10231–38. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1500012112.
Anderson, S., A. T. Bankier, B. G. Barrell, et al. 1981. “Sequence and Organization of the Human Mitochondrial Genome.” Nature 290 (5806): 457–65. https://doi.org/10.1038/290457a0.
Babayev, Elnur, and Emre Seli. 2015. “Oocyte Mitochondrial Function and Reproduction.” Current Opinion in Obstetrics & Gynecology 27 (3): 175–81. https://doi.org/10.1097/GCO.0000000000000164.
Roger, Andrew J., Sergio A. Muñoz-Gómez, and Ryoma Kamikawa. 2017. “The Origin and Diversification of Mitochondria.” Current Biology 27 (21): R1177–92. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cub.2017.09.015.
Sutovsky, P., R. D. Moreno, J. Ramalho-Santos, T. Dominko, C. Simerly, and G. Schatten. 1999. “Ubiquitin Tag for Sperm Mitochondria.” Nature 402 (6760): 371–72. https://doi.org/10.1038/46466.

item.title: Weeks 1–2: first, set up the calendar
item.description:
No one has pushed a hotfix to the genome yet, so I’m reading the legacy code.

What I did

  • Started Essence of Linear Algebra by 3Blue1Brown and got through six of the videos.
  • Began MIT Missing Semester — the shell lecture.
  • Studied High School Biology every single day on Khan Academy, 30–35 minutes each day.
  • Set up this blog: Quarto, a GitHub repo, and a lot of time spent picking a logo (obviously, the top importance).
  • Ran three times a week and did two strength sessions each week. Because the golden rule is: the more you stress your brain, the more you should stress your body (in the common sense of the word).

What clicked

Biology happened every day, the code part barely happened at all. The key difference was that the biology has its own time slot in my calendar before work, when my mind is mostly fresh. So time-management is everything when you have too much stuff to think about.

Where I got stuck

3Blue1Brown explains linear algebra through geometry, and my brain doesn’t do spatial pictures. I was even questioning my own knowledge about these concepts, because visual transformations of matrices made everything much more complicated. For example, I understand that the determinant is the area of the parallelogram formed by two adjacent vectors, but the narrator does rotations, scaling, or shearing of axes — and I am lost in the deep forest of geometry. Not to mention the 3D planes.

For a while I thought this was a problem I had to fix. Then I realized that in bioengineering I’ll be working with data in hundreds of dimensions that nobody can picture anyway. So I’m treating it as a known weak spot and moving on.

What I’m changing

Every task now gets a time block in a weekly calendar, with a start and an end. Studying moves to the morning, before work, where it’s already proven its efficiency. But also I have an hour after work, but for more relaxing studying tasks.

Next week

  • Missing Semester (lectures 2 — 7)
  • The Linux Command Line (chapters 1–5)
  • Python for Data Analysis (chapters 1–2)
  • Solve some Rosalind problems
  • Mock IELTS
  • High School Biology every day
  • 3Blue1Brown (lessons 7–16)

item.title: The plan: fifteen weeks to January
item.description:
Every plan survives until the first Monday.

I came up with a huge plan for the new year. But what do I do with the four months before it? There’s no point in sitting around waiting for January. So I decided to take some of the weight off next year and start now.

What I’m learning

In this order, because each step leans on the one before:

  1. MIT Missing Semester — filling the gaps. After eight years I use git and the shell every day, but mostly the same ten commands. Bioinformatics lives in the terminal, so it’s time to learn these tools properly.
  2. The Linux Command Line, parts 1–2 — going deeper while the terminal is fresh.
  3. Python for Data Analysis, chapters 1–10 — NumPy and pandas.
  4. Rosalind — 30 bioinformatics problems to practise Python on real tasks.
  5. R for Data Science — the tidyverse and plotting.
  6. Harvard Stat 110, lectures 1–17 — probability.
  7. Essential Cell Biology (Alberts), chapters 1–9, alongside MITx The Secret of Life.

Biology runs alongside all of this every morning, on Khan Academy. I finished Middle School Biology over the summer, I’m now working through High School Biology, and AP/College Biology comes next — maybe chemistry after that. I also started a Harvard course on mitochondria earlier, and I’d like to come back to it once the basics are in place.

And linear algebra with 3Blue1Brown — taking it slowly. Geometry is my weak spot, and these videos are worth watching carefully rather than quickly.

What I’m building

  • This blog, with a weekly log every Monday.
  • My first pull request to an open-source project.
  • A small project in December: one public dataset, from raw data to a few clear plots, all in Python.
